outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with the SF Treasurer for a Business Registration Certificate, and file a Fictitious Business Name statement if the DBA differs from the legal entity name. What to say: Register online with the SF Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector within 30 days of starting business; the fee is tiered by gross receipts (e.g., $55 up to $100k, $95 up to $250k, each plus a $4 state fee) and the registration year runs April 1 to March 31. You will receive a Business Account Number (BAN) needed for all other city permits. If the public-facing name (e.g., Ristorante Ideale) differs from the legal entity name, file a Fictitious Business Name statement with the County Clerk in person or by mail with photo ID, then publish in a court-approved newspaper once a week for four weeks and file proof of publication within 45 days (total cost $60–$120). The FBN statement is required by ABC and most banks.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a California Seller's Permit (sales tax) and an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if not already held. What to say: Apply online with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) for a seller's permit; there is no fee and it is often issued the same day. ABC requires the seller's permit before issuing a liquor license. If the business does not yet have a federal EIN, apply online with the IRS (free, issued immediately Mon–Fri); the EIN is needed to open a business bank account, register for payroll taxes, and apply for the ABC license. Also register with the California Employment Development Department (EDD) for payroll taxes within 15 days of paying more than $100 in wages in a quarter (free, online, takes 1–7 days); your payroll provider needs the EDD account number.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Ensure all employees obtain California Food Handler Cards and that at least one manager holds a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate. What to say: Every employee who handles food must obtain a California Food Handler Card within 30 days of hire from an ANSI-accredited online course (about $7–$15, valid 3 years); the online course takes about two hours. At least one owner or employee must pass an accredited food safety certification exam (ServSafe, Prometric, NRFSP, or 360training) and hold a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate within 60 days of opening; DPH asks for this certificate at the pre-opening inspection (course plus exam about $100–$250, valid 5 years). All alcohol servers and their managers must complete Responsible Beverage Service (RBS) certification within 60 days of hire: register on the ABC RBS Portal ($3), complete an approved course (about $10–$25), and pass the exam; keep the certification list on site for ABC inspections.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain workers' compensation insurance, ASCAP and BMI music licenses, and subscribe to organics recycling service before opening. What to say: Workers' compensation insurance is mandatory from the first employee (even part-time); quote through a broker or the State Compensation Insurance Fund and provide proof of coverage to DPH and the Entertainment Commission if needed. Subscribe to ASCAP and BMI public performance licenses ($300–$2,500 each per year, formula-based on occupancy and music use) to cover background music and any live or recorded music played publicly; sign up online and the licenses are effective immediately. Set up organics (green bin) collection service with your hauler before opening (required under SB 1383 for all food businesses); the city enforces it through the business license or health inspection.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 90 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $18,000 to $453,000. Notes: The time and cost ranges are for the approvals in the entitlement path when they are granted: Conditional Use Authorization (if required), Health Permit to Operate, and Building Permit (if building work is proposed). The CUA timeline is 120–300 days from filing to approval (based on the catalog entry for sf.conditional_use_authorization, which is not in this catalog but is consistent with the 9-month approval at 414 Columbus Ave, app:datasf_planning:2022-002108CUA); the Health Permit is 14–45 days (catalog:sf.health_permit); the Building Permit for work without a change of use is 14–120 days (catalog:sf.building_permit, though not formally in the path because no tenant improvements are stated). The government cost includes the ABC Type 47 license transfer or purchase ($17,000–$450,000, catalog:ca.abc_type_47), the CUA application fee (approximately $3,100, not in the catalog but stated in the sf.conditional_use_authorization notes), the Health Permit application ($470, catalog:sf.health_permit), and city/state registration fees (business registration $55–$700, seller's permit $0, EDD $0, entity registration $70–$150, catalog entries). The ranges assume the Type 47 is acquired by transfer; if the existing license (ABC #372058) is still active and continues, the cost drops to the lower end (no license purchase, only the transfer filing fee of roughly $1,000–$1,600). If Planning determines that no new CUA is required because the 1988 authorization remains in effect and the project is a continuation, the timeline drops to 90–120 days (ABC transfer plus health permit) and the cost to $17,000–$18,000. These figures are times and costs to approval; they do not cover a denial or a withdrawal. The ABC license transfer timeline (90–240 days) includes escrow, posting, ABC investigation, and local agency referrals but assumes no protest or Public Convenience or Necessity (PCN) hearing; a protest or PCN finding would add 1–3 months. No tenant improvements are stated, so no building permit time or cost is included unless construction is proposed. Confirm the pathway with Planning before incurring costs.

The ranges assume the Type 47 is acquired by transfer; if the existing license (ABC #372058) is still active and continues, the cost drops to the lower end (no license purchase, only the transfer filing fee of roughly $1,000–$1,600). If Planning determines that no new CUA is required because the 1988 authorization remains in effect and the project is a continuation, the timeline drops to 90–120 days (ABC transfer plus health permit) and the cost to $17,000–$18,000. These figures are times and costs to approval; they do not cover a denial or a withdrawal. The ABC license transfer timeline (90–240 days) includes escrow, posting, ABC investigation, and local agency referrals but assumes no protest or Public Convenience or Necessity (PCN) hearing; a protest or PCN finding would add 1–3 months. No tenant improvements are stated, so no building permit time or cost is included unless construction is proposed. Confirm the pathway with Planning before incurring costs.
